title: Hymn 4, sound: kaam karodh
hook: kaam karodh nagar bahu bhariaa (Gauri Purbi M4, ang 13)

segments.voice: Yesterday, pavan, the wind; your line was the whole world offering. Today the mood changes: hymn four.

A new voice enters Sohila tonight. The first three hymns were Guru Nanak's. The fourth is by Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, whom Sikhs remember as the founder of the town that grew into Amritsar. Someone who founds a town learns how one fills up, street by street. So it fits that his hymn is about a crowded town. Only this town isn't on any map. It's a body at the end of a long day, with whatever it's still carrying.
screen: `A NEW VOICE: GURU RAM DAS.` → `A TOWN, AND A CROWDED ONE.` → `THE FIRST LINE IS A WARNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the line: kaam karodh nagar bahu bhariaa. Word by word. Kaam: desire that has run out of control, lust, craving. Karodh: anger. Nagar: a town, a city. Bahu: very much. Bhariaa: filled. So: the city is crammed with desire and anger. The city is the body, and the mind that lives in it, its streets full of two restless characters who never seem to sleep. Then the line finishes, and the warning becomes a hope. In paraphrase: meeting the holy, they are broken to pieces. The holy here is saadhoo, the person who has truly given themselves to God, and some readers hear in it the sangat, the company of people who sing God's praise together. So the hymn doesn't pretend the city is quiet. It names the crowd, and it names what breaks it up. The hymn is in Raag Gauri Purbi, on Ang 13, right after Guru Nanak's three. Listen to its sound: kaam and karodh both open on a hard k. The line begins with a jolt, like a door banged at night, hard to sleep through. Tomorrow, the rest of the city's residents. Today, two loud names, a crowded town, and the promise that the crowd can be broken.
screen: `KAAM: CRAVING. KARODH: ANGER.` · `NAGAR: THE CITY OF THE BODY.` · `MEETING THE HOLY, THEY BREAK.` · `A LINE THAT OPENS WITH A JOLT.` · then, large: `KAAM KARODH.`

segments.voice: Say the line once, clearly, feeling the two hard k sounds: kaam karodh nagar bahu bhariaa. Then sit and notice, without judging, whether either one is in your city right now, a little irritation, a craving, the way you'd notice a car passing outside. Let your shoulders drop, and if you pray, say Waheguru once.
Krodh, anger: Sohila's fourth hymn, by Guru Ram Das, the city of the body is crammed with desire and anger, and meeting the holy, they are broken.
Your line: kaam karodh. Desire and anger, named, and not the last word. Day four hundred thirty.

howItsDone: This is the fourth of the five hymns Sikhs recite every night in Kirtan Sohila; it is Guru Ram Das's, and it follows the three hymns of Guru Nanak.

chat.says: Sohila's fourth hymn says the city is crammed with desire and anger. What breaks them up?
options: Meeting the holy: in the hymn's words, in that company they're broken to pieces.
Willpower alone, fighting them by yourself until they finally give up.
Nothing; the hymn says the city simply stays crowded for good.
